The five fakes highlighted in a different colour and corrected in the margin. This page makes us trustworthy by admitting what gets misquoted, including by us.

what: #97 — fixed vs growth mindset drawn as the identical four puzzle pieces, once locked shut and once open
mech: One object drawn twice, with only one property changed. The whole argument is in the difference, and no sentence is needed.
ours: The identical rock drawn twice, same size, same shading. Labelled A PILLOW and A PILLAR. Nothing about the stone changed between the two drawings — only the night in between, and what he did with it in the morning.

what: Weekly Bingo for tiny achievements · January's Inner Work — a hand-drawn grid you circle
mech: Things too small to count as achievements, which is exactly why ticking them feels good. It becomes yours the moment you mark it.
ours: Twenty-five squares of ordinary faithfulness nobody claps for: told the truth when a lie was easier · let someone go first · said sorry first · didn't say the thing · read one verse · sat with somebody who was sad · asked for help. Free square in the middle: you woke up.

what: #102 — a postbox on a wall beside a rack of tear-off cards: leave your impression behind, drop the card in
mech: Two actions, not one. You take something AND you give something back, anonymously, and the wall keeps both.
ours: Stronger than the tear-off page on its own. A perforated strip of notes to take, and directly beside it a card to fill in and post back — the address printed on it. What comes back becomes page 28 of the next issue. The paper stops being a broadcast.
where: Its own page, near the Spine

what: #103 — The Creative Manifesto: hand-lettered centred lines inside a thick wobbling blue border
mech: The wobble is the whole personality. A straight frame would make it corporate; the hand-drawn one makes it a gift.
ours: Same treatment for the twelve-line Between Sundays manifesto — hand-lettered, centred, inside a wobbling border in one of our inks. Every line is a verse in plain speech with its reference set tiny underneath. It is designed to be torn out and stuck on a wall.

what: Beyrouth aux usines Abroyan — a two-ink cultural programme: dated columns, numbered session tags, portraits, dense but perfectly gridded
mech: A festival's whole week in one poster; the tags and dates make density navigable.
ours: 'SEVEN DAYS AT BETHEL' — the Spine's week redesigned as a festival programme: each day a session tag (DAY 1 · SUNDOWN · free admission), speakers listed (God — no advance booking), venue notes (one field, no seating). The programme format makes the reading plan feel like an event you're attending.

what: The typed poem to a piano with red circles/highlights, the object photographed below — the piece behind our marked-up page concept
mech: Typed text + hand markup + the object underneath. The markup is a second reader arguing with the first.
ours: Confirmed as the visual control for the p05 marked-up page (already concepted with the six corrections). The addition this original teaches: the OBJECT below should be plain and domestic — our rock, photographed like a product, dead centre.

what: 'Banksy said / Matisse said…' — twenty artists, one line each, hand-lettered in a rough grid, no quote bigger than another
mech: Democratic grid: every voice gets the same cell, so the page reads as a chorus rather than a headline.
ours: 'WHAT PEOPLE SAID IN THE DARK' (already concepted) — this is its visual control. Each cell one line from someone at their lowest, hand-lettered, with the reference: JOB SAID the day I was born should be erased · DAVID SAID how long must I wrestle with my thoughts · ELIJAH SAID I have had enough · JESUS SAID my God, why have you abandoned me. Nothing resolved on the page; the resolution is that every speaker was kept.

what: 'Storytelling + Artists — Terminator Studies' — a two-ink conspiracy map: portraits, logos, dates, red threads all leading to one node
mech: Overwhelming connection rendered credible by museum coolness. The single centre node organises the chaos.
ours: 'EVERYTHING HE WAS TOLD TO CARRY' (already concepted as the promise board) — upgraded by this reference: two-ink screenprint style, portraits as halftone blocks, dates on the threads. Abraham (Gen 12:2) → Isaac (Gen 26:24) → Jacob (Gen 28:13) — the SAME promise, word-for-word overlaps highlighted, all threads converging on one small sleeping figure. J.G. Ballard's caption slot becomes Hebrews 11:13 — 'they saw it all from a distance.'
where: A spread — the most ambitious page in the issue

what: 'Dopamine Menu' — self-care activities formatted as appetizers/entrees/desserts
mech: The menu metaphor sorts habits by cost and payoff.
ours: Skip for the paper — self-optimisation content; our menu slot is taken by Isaiah 55 (THE TABLE), which does the same format with scripture as the source. Keep in the workspace for Life/health if useful.
skipwhy: Self-optimisation genre; the menu format is already ours via Isaiah 55

what: A physically cut/torn magazine page — most words excised, survivors forming a raw argument about God and justice, photo showing through the holes
mech: Physical destruction as composition: the page bleeds through its own wounds, and the surviving words carry the weight.
ours: THE BLACKOUT AD, physical edition — instead of printed black bars, the John 16:29-33 page is CUT: every non-surviving word razored out, the butter-yellow sheet behind showing through the holes, so the light literally comes through where words were removed. Surviving words: YOU ARE NOT ALONE / I AM WITH YOU. Photograph the cut object; print the photograph. Honest craft, no digital redaction.
where: The full-page ad — this beats the printed-bar version

what: 'The Design Thinking Process' — the tangled scribble resolving into a straight line
mech: One continuous line tells the whole story; everyone recognises their own life in it.
ours: Already concepted as 'The line from Beersheba' — this is its control. Labels: Beersheba in the knot · the stone mid-tangle · Bethel where it straightens · twenty years along the flat. Caption: most of this drawing is the part nobody writes down.

what: Nike's internal 10 principles, 1977 — typewriter, one page, 'It won't be pretty'
mech: Zero design. The typewriter voice IS the authority; you believe it because nobody prettied it up.
ours: The Between Sundays manifesto gets TWO forms: the wavy-border tear-out (already concepted) and THIS — the internal typewritten version pinned in the workspace and printed small on p02: '1. We are messengers, not experts. 2. Everything sourced or it doesn't print. 3. Doubt is allowed in the room…' If the wavy one is for readers' walls, this one is for ours.

what: Bruce Mau's 'An Incomplete Manifesto for Growth' — 43 numbered permissions filling a yellow page, one left blank
mech: Numbered abundance: too many rules to obey, so they read as permissions. Number 17 is blank on purpose.
ours: 'AN INCOMPLETE MANIFESTO FOR THE MIDDLE OF THE WEEK' — forty-three numbered permissions on butter yellow, every one sourced: 1. Stop for the night (Gen 28:11). 2. Use what's there (the stone). 3. Sleep is not quitting (Ps 127:2). 4. Doubt out loud (Mark 9:24). 5. Complain first (Ps 13)… and one number left blank with a rule: ____ — yours, write it in. The blank one is the whole invitation.

what: 'The Porch Light Theory' — red handwriting, yellow highlighter on the lines that matter
mech: Handwriting + someone else's highlighter = you are reading a note that was already loved by a previous reader.
ours: Control for the marked-up page family. Our version of THIS specific piece: 'The Light Stays On' rewritten from the actual source — the father in Luke 15 saw his son 'while he was still a long way off', which means he was WATCHING THE ROAD. Handwritten, with the highlighter on: 'you cannot ruin what is meant for you by taking longer to find it' becomes 'he saw him while he was still a long way off — which means the light was never off.'
where: Page 05 family or a Spine page

what: 'Occam's Razor' — rule, plain-English gloss, household example, one doodle, italic maxim at the foot
mech: One rule per page, one dumb example, one drawing. Endlessly serialisable.
ours: Control for 'Rules for reading the Bible without getting it wrong' (already concepted). The household-example move is the part to keep: 'If it makes you feel superior, re-read it. If you hear a meowing under the sofa, it's probably the cat — and if a verse makes you the hero, it's probably not about you.'

what: '1000 Hours Outside' — an illustrated header over a thousand tiny cells you colour in across a year
mech: The grid makes an abstract commitment physical: every cell you fill is proof, and the poster becomes a diary.
ours: 'ONE CHAPTER AT A TIME' — a colour-in tracker of every chapter in the Bible: 1,189 tiny cells under an illustrated header (the road from Beersheba running through mountains to a city). No schedule, no dates, no streaks — just cells. Fill them in any order over any number of years. The anti-app reading plan; the poster IS the testimony when it's full.
where: Full page or a Spine pull-out — strong merch candidate too

what: 'Alternatives to How Are You?' — the hand-lettered question grid (second copy)
ours: Already concepted as 'What to say when somebody is grieving'. This copy confirms the grid treatment: 35 cells, a few tinted, one cell that just says {Just Listen} — ours keeps that exact cell: {Job 2:13 — just sit}.
skipwhy: Duplicate of the concepted grieving-grid reference

what: A Robinson Crusoe page with words boxed and connected by drawn lines, start → end, making a hidden path
mech: A maze built ON a book page: the reader travels word to word, and the chosen words form a second text.
ours: Our connect-the-dots page grown up: print Genesis 28 in full (it's on p08 anyway), then a START arrow — the reader draws lines box to box through: STOPPED → STONE → DREAMED → STAIRWAY → WITH YOU → WHEREVER → AWAKE → SURELY → HOUSE OF GOD. The path through the passage IS the summary of the passage, and you cannot find it without reading every line. Answer path on p46 upside down.
where: Games block (p31-32) — replaces or joins the crossword

what: 'Workplace Alternatives to How Are You?' — the same grid format, work edition
mech: Same democratic cell grid; proves the format serialises by context.
ours: Confirms the grieving-grid can be a SERIES: what to say when somebody is grieving · when somebody got bad news · when somebody comes back to church after years. One format, many mercies. Keep {Just listen} as the constant cell in every edition.

what: 'One Man's Trash / Another's Treasure' — a plain chair mid-page, hundreds of scrawled opinions radiating off it
mech: The object stays still; the noise swirls. Every opinion is legible if you lean in, ignorable if you don't.
ours: Control for THE STONE radial (already concepted). One addition from seeing it properly: the two halves are TITLED — one side 'one man's trash', the other 'another's treasure'. Ours titles the halves A PILLOW / A PILLAR, so the radial argument has an axis.

what: 'The Cultural Iceberg' — visible culture above the waterline, deep culture below
mech: The waterline splits the seen from the unseen.
ours: Skip for the paper as-is (classroom infographic), but the WATERLINE mechanic is worth holding: what people see of a believer (Sunday, the habits) vs what carries it underneath (the doubts, the discipline, the kept promises). If it ever runs, it's drawn as our own object — not an iceberg.
skipwhy: Classroom-infographic genre; keep the waterline idea, not the page

t: The raft on a sea of words
what: A tiny photographed figure on a raft, floating on an ocean made of thousands of cut newspaper fragments
mech: Scale contrast: one real person adrift on infinite chopped-up language. The sea is literally made of noise.
ours: 'ALL THE ADVICE' — one small figure on a raft, and the entire sea is cut-up fragments of everything the world tells you (hustle harder · manifest it · you're enough · five easy steps · new year new you), thousands of them, all real clippings. One line of clear water at the horizon: 'Come to me, all of you who are weary.' The only sentence that isn't chopped.
where: Full page — one of the strongest single images available to us

what: Musgrave Pencil Co. — a 1960s trade catalogue page: each pencil photographed flat, numbered, deadpan specs
mech: The catalogue's flatness IS the charm. Numbered SKUs, no hierarchy, complete confidence the object deserves documentation.
ours: 'INSTRUMENTS OF RECORD' — the writing tools of scripture as a specimen page: No. 1 THE FINGER (wrote on stone — Exodus 31:18, and on a wall — Daniel 5:5) · No. 2 THE IRON PEN (Job 19:24 — 'engraved forever in the rock') · No. 3 THE REED PEN (3 John 13) · No. 4 THE STYLUS (Isaiah 8:1). Deadpan specs for each. Ends: No. 5 — YOURS. See page 43.
where: Near the notebook page — the field guide series

what: 'Once in a House on Fire' — a real matchbook as the book cover, matches unstruck, the title in a smoke-shaped thought bubble
mech: One object photographed straight; the drawing completes what the object implies. Nothing else on the cover.
ours: Already concepted as the stone-with-ladder cover. This original confirms the recipe: REAL object (a stone), one drawn continuation (the stairway as a pencil line rising off it), title in the drawn element. Also the Isaiah 42:3 version: a photographed matchbook with every match struck except one — 'he will not put out a flickering candle.'

what: 'A Gentle Reminder' p81 — a book page where a previous reader's four highlighter colours and red underlines do the arguing
mech: Multiple highlight colours = multiple readings, or one reader at different times. The page carries its own history of being needed.
ours: 'THE PSALM EVERYBODY MARKED' — Psalm 23 printed once, carrying four readers' marks in four colours, with a small key: yellow = read at a funeral · pink = taped to a hospital bed · blue = memorised at eight years old · green = came back to it last week. Same text, four lives. The key row makes it a testimony page without a single testimony written out.
where: Full page — Reading section or Spine
